audit.reasoning: Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim in the held excerpt and in the full local extracted text of the open-access book at sec. 2.2, p. 22 (page confirmed by the book index), and the endnote is verbatim too. Deciding source: a 2021 reference grammar, but of the sister dialect Akajeru, and the stress sentence is a blanket family-wide claim by authors working from early-1900s transcriptions that (as they say themselves) never marked stress; the same book documents that traditional Akakhora survives only as a handful of nouns and toponyms, so for Aka-Kora the root-initial claim is inference. Glottolog lists exactly two descriptive refs for akak1251 (Yadav 1985 sketch; Abbi 2006 sketch); neither was consulted by the catalog readers. I downloaded Yadav 1985 (open, SEAlang; image PDF, scanned at 300 dpi and checked against the page image): his main informant was a Kora-group man, and he writes

sources.quote: "The accent is very weak and does not appear to be phonemic. Whatever weak accent there is, usually falls on the first syllable. There is, however, an exception: a strong accent marks the final syllable of vocatives and exclamations." Examples: ṭeṭe 'hungry' vs ṭe'ṭe' 'hey! listen!', Tawo 'ghost' vs Ta'wo 'naughty!', ekaye 'bad' vs eka'ye 'wrong!'. p. 188: "I decided to record primarily one language and to rely on one person, Pikar, who belongs to the Kora group of the G.A." (language recorded is present-day mixed Great Andamanese, 'similar to the examples of the Aka-jeru group').
